prompt: Under the federal standard, you need a CDL to drive a single vehicle with a gross vehicle weight rating (GVWR) of at least:
choices: 20,000 pounds
33,001 pounds
26,001 pounds
10,001 pounds
explanation: A CDL is required for any single vehicle with a GVWR of 26,001 pounds or more. Some states add more vehicles, but none require less.

prompt: A pickup with a 14,000-lb GVWR tows a trailer with a 14,000-lb GVWR. Under the federal classes, which CDL covers this combination?
choices: Class A
No CDL, because neither unit is over 26,000 pounds
Class C
Class B
explanation: Class A covers combinations with a GCWR of 26,001 pounds or more when the towed unit's GVWR is over 10,000 pounds. Here the GCWR is 28,000 pounds and the trailer is 14,000 pounds.

prompt: A straight truck with a 30,000-lb GVWR tows a small trailer with an 8,000-lb GVWR. Which CDL class fits this vehicle?
choices: No CDL class applies
Class B
Class A
Class C
explanation: Class B is a single vehicle of 26,001 pounds GVWR or more, or such a vehicle towing a unit of not more than 10,000 pounds GVWR. The trailer is too light to make it Class A.

prompt: Under the federal standard, a vehicle lighter than 26,001 lbs GVWR still needs a CDL if it is designed to carry how many people, counting the driver?
choices: 8 or more
16 or more
10 or more
24 or more
explanation: A vehicle designed to carry 16 or more passengers, including the driver, requires a CDL. Some states set a lower number, but the federal standard is 16.

prompt: Which endorsements are the only ones that may be added to a Commercial Learner's Permit (CLP)?
choices: Passenger, School Bus, and Tank Vehicle
Hazardous Materials, Tank Vehicle, and Doubles/Triples
Doubles/Triples, Passenger, and Tank Vehicle
Passenger, Hazardous Materials, and School Bus
explanation: Only the Passenger (P), School Bus (S), and Tank Vehicle (N) endorsements may be placed on a CLP. Hazardous Materials and Doubles/Triples cannot.

prompt: Which CDL endorsement shows that a driver has passed both the tank vehicle and the hazardous materials knowledge tests?
choices: H
T
X
N
explanation: The X endorsement combines Tank Vehicle (N) and Hazardous Materials (H). T is for double and triple trailers.

prompt: The CDL skills test is made up of which three parts?
choices: Vehicle inspection, basic control, and on-road test
Written knowledge test, backing test, and highway driving test
Vehicle inspection, cargo loading test, and on-road driving test
Air brake check, night driving test, and on-road driving test
explanation: The skills test has three segments taken in order: vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, and the on-road test. You must pass each one before moving to the next.

prompt: It is illegal to operate a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) if your blood alcohol concentration (BAC) is:
choices: 0.02% or more
0.08% or more
0.04% or more
0.10% or more
explanation: For CMV drivers the limit is 0.04% BAC, half of the 0.08% limit most states use for car drivers.

prompt: A CMV driver is found to have a detectable amount of alcohol, but a BAC below 0.04%. What happens?
choices: The driver loses the CDL for one year
The driver is put out of service for 24 hours
The driver is put out of service for 8 hours
Nothing, because the BAC is under the limit
explanation: Any detectable amount of alcohol under 0.04% puts a CMV driver out of service for 24 hours. Being under 0.04% only avoids the longer disqualification.

prompt: For a first offense of driving a CMV with a BAC of 0.04% or higher, a driver loses the CDL for at least:
choices: Life
Three years
One year
60 days
explanation: A first alcohol offense in a CMV brings at least a one-year disqualification. It rises to three years if the vehicle was placarded for hazardous materials, and a second offense means life.

prompt: A driver's first alcohol offense happens while driving a CMV placarded for hazardous materials. What is the minimum disqualification?
choices: Five years
One year
Life
Three years
explanation: The usual one-year minimum for a first offense becomes at least three years when the CMV was placarded for hazardous materials.

prompt: Which offense results in losing your CDL for life even if it is your first one?
choices: Using a CMV to commit a felony involving controlled substances
Refusing to take an alcohol test when asked while driving a CMV
Driving a CMV while your CDL is suspended or revoked
Leaving the scene of an accident while driving a CMV
explanation: Using a CMV to commit a felony involving controlled substances means a lifetime loss of the CDL. The other offenses bring at least one year for a first offense and life for a second.

prompt: Speeding counts as a serious traffic violation for a CDL holder when you drive how far over the posted limit?
choices: 15 mph or more
5 mph or more
10 mph or more
20 mph or more
explanation: Excessive speeding, defined as 15 mph or more above the posted limit, is a serious traffic violation.

prompt: Two serious traffic violations in a CMV within a three-year period lead to a CDL disqualification of at least:
choices: One year
30 days
60 days
120 days
explanation: Two serious violations within three years means at least 60 days. Three or more within three years means at least 120 days.

prompt: A CDL holder is convicted for the first time of a railroad-highway grade crossing violation in a CMV. The minimum disqualification is:
choices: 60 days
30 days
120 days
One year
explanation: A first railroad crossing violation brings at least 60 days. A second within three years is at least 120 days, and a third is at least one year.

prompt: You are convicted of a moving violation while driving your personal car. Within how many days must you tell your employer?
choices: 2 business days
90 days
10 days
30 days
explanation: You must notify your employer within 30 days of a conviction for any traffic violation except parking, no matter what type of vehicle you were driving.

prompt: When you apply for a commercial driving job, you must give the employer information about all driving jobs you held during the past:
choices: 7 years
3 years
5 years
10 years
explanation: Applicants must list all driving jobs held in the past 10 years.

prompt: How many driver licenses may a commercial driver hold?
choices: One for each class of vehicle they drive
Only one, from your home state
One for each state where they drive
Two: a CDL and a separate car license
explanation: You may not have more than one license. A court can fine you up to $5,000 or jail you, keep your home state license, and return any others. All states share a computer system to check for this.

prompt: What is the most important reason for inspecting your vehicle?
choices: Safety, for yourself and other road users
Avoiding fines from roadside inspectors
Meeting your employer's paperwork rules
Keeping the vehicle's resale value up
explanation: Safety is the most important reason to inspect. A defect found early can prevent a breakdown or a crash.

prompt: If a federal or state inspector judges your vehicle to be unsafe, what will happen?
choices: It will be put out of service until it is fixed
You will get a warning and may finish the trip
You must drive it straight to a repair shop
Your CDL will be suspended for 30 days
explanation: Inspectors who find a vehicle unsafe will put it out of service until it is repaired.

prompt: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove of a front tire?
choices: 4/32 inch
1/32 inch
6/32 inch
2/32 inch
explanation: Front tires need at least 4/32 inch of tread in every major groove. Other tires need at least 2/32 inch.

prompt: What is the minimum tread depth for tires other than the front tires?
choices: 2/32 inch
1/32 inch
3/32 inch
4/32 inch
explanation: Tires other than the front tires need at least 2/32 inch of tread. The front tires need 4/32 inch.

prompt: Which kind of tire is NOT allowed on the front wheels of a bus?
choices: Recapped, retreaded, or re-grooved tires
Radial tires
Tubeless tires
Tires made by a different brand than the rear tires
explanation: Re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus.

prompt: What should you do a short while after a tire has been changed?
choices: Let some air out of the new tire
Avoid braking hard until the next oil change
Wait until the end of the trip to check the lug nuts
Stop and re-check the tightness of the wheel nuts
explanation: After a tire change, stop a short while later and re-check the wheel nuts. They can loosen as the wheel settles.

prompt: Which wheel or rim condition is considered unsafe?
choices: A rim with no visible rust
A rim with a fresh coat of paint
A wheel with all its lugs in place
A rim that has had welding repairs
explanation: Wheels or rims that have had welding repairs are not safe. Missing clamps, studs, or lugs and bent or cracked lock rings are also dangerous.

prompt: How much steering wheel play is too much?
choices: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches on a 20-inch wheel)
More than 45 degrees (about 8 inches at the rim of the wheel)
More than 25 degrees (about 5 inches at the rim of the wheel)
More than 2 degrees (less than half an inch at the rim)
explanation: Play of more than 10 degrees, about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel, can make it hard to steer.

prompt: A leaf spring has some missing leaves. When will the vehicle be put out of service?
choices: When one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing
Only when half or more of the leaves are missing
Never; leaf springs are not checked at inspections
Only when every leaf on one side is broken
explanation: If one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing, the vehicle will be put out of service. Even so, any spring defect could be dangerous.

prompt: Why is a broken exhaust system dangerous?
choices: It drains the batteries faster than normal
It makes the engine lose power on steep upgrades
It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper
It causes the engine to run too cold in winter
explanation: A broken exhaust system can let poison fumes, such as carbon monoxide, into the cab or sleeper berth.

prompt: Which of these is required emergency equipment on a commercial vehicle?
choices: Tire chains, a spare tire, a jack, and a first-aid kit
A flashlight, jumper cables, and a heavy tow strap
A fire extinguisher, spare fuses, and warning devices
Road flares, a snow shovel, and spare light bulbs
explanation: Required emergency equipment is a fire extinguisher, spare electrical fuses (unless the vehicle has circuit breakers), and warning devices for parked vehicles. Chains and tire tools are optional items.

prompt: Which set of warning devices meets the requirement for a parked commercial vehicle?
choices: Three red reflective triangles
One triangle and two flashlights
Two red reflective triangles
Three orange traffic cones
explanation: You need three reflective triangles, or at least six fuses, or three liquid-burning flares.

prompt: Your truck is carrying hazardous materials. Besides checking that the cargo is secure, what must you inspect for?
choices: A receipt showing the cargo was weighed twice
A tarp covering all of the cargo
Proper shipping papers and placards
A tank endorsement on your CDL
explanation: If the cargo includes hazardous materials, you must inspect for proper papers and placarding.

prompt: You review the previous driver's inspection report. When are you required to sign it?
choices: Only if you find new defects of your own during inspection
Every time you take the vehicle, even when no defects were reported
Only if listed defects were certified as repaired or not needed
Never; only the mechanic who made the repairs signs it
explanation: The carrier must repair reported safety defects and certify the repair. You sign the report only if defects were noted and certified as repaired or not needed.

prompt: Before you check the engine compartment, what should you make sure of?
choices: The headlights and four-way flashers are turned on
The engine is running at high idle to keep the oil warm
The parking brake is set and/or the wheels are chocked
The transmission is in reverse with the clutch released
explanation: Check that the parking brakes are on and/or the wheels are chocked before working in the engine compartment.

prompt: After you start the engine during the inspection, what should the ABS warning light on the dash do?
choices: Stay on as long as the engine runs
Flash until you release the parking brake
Come on and then go off
Never light up at all
explanation: The ABS light should come on and then turn off. If it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.

prompt: After the engine is started, how soon should oil pressure come up to normal?
choices: Within seconds
Within about 3 minutes
Once the coolant is fully warm
After a few miles of driving
explanation: Oil pressure should come up to normal within seconds after the engine starts. Coolant and oil temperature rise gradually.

prompt: In Section 2's engine-start check, air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within about how long?
choices: 10 minutes
3 minutes
1 minute
15 seconds
explanation: Section 2 says pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes, then up to governor cut-out (usually about 120-140 psi). Section 5 adds that modern dual air systems should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds.

prompt: During the walk-around, what color should clearance lights and reflectors at the front be?
choices: Red
White
Amber
Blue
explanation: Parking, clearance, and identification lights and reflectors at the front should be amber. Those at the rear should be red.

prompt: What color should side-marker lights and reflectors at the rear of the vehicle be?
choices: Amber
Red
White
Green
explanation: Side-marker lights and reflectors are red at the rear and amber elsewhere.

prompt: How do you check a hydraulic brake system for leaks during the inspection?
choices: Pump the pedal 10 times quickly and check that it gets softer with each push
Pump the pedal 3 times, then hold firm pressure 5 seconds; it shouldn't move
Hold light pressure for 30 seconds and watch the brake fluid gauge
Press the pedal once and listen for a hissing sound near each wheel
explanation: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold it for five seconds. If the pedal moves, there may be a leak or other problem.

prompt: How should you test the parking brake during your inspection?
choices: Set it and press hard on the service brake pedal at the same time
Set it, shift to a low gear, and gently pull forward against it
Set it, shift to neutral, and rev the engine to see if the vehicle moves
Release it while rolling slowly downhill at about 5 mph
explanation: With the parking brake set, place the vehicle in a low gear and gently pull forward against it. If it doesn't hold, it is faulty.

prompt: When you test your service brakes, the vehicle pulls to one side. What does this suggest?
choices: The tires are properly inflated
The road is crowned, which is normal
The ABS is working correctly
There may be brake trouble
explanation: Pulling to one side during the brake test can mean brake trouble. Get it fixed, because it is illegal to operate an unsafe vehicle.

prompt: When hauling cargo in a truck, when must you first check the cargo securement, and how often after that?
choices: Within the first 25 miles, then every 2 hours or 100 miles
Within the first 100 miles, then every 4 hours or 200 miles
Within the first 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles
Within the first 50 miles, then every 6 hours or 300 miles
explanation: Check cargo securement within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first.

prompt: During a trip, you smell something unusual. What should you do?
choices: Speed up to reach the terminal sooner
Wait to see whether it gets worse
Note it in the after-trip report and keep going
Stop safely and check it out
explanation: If you see, hear, smell, or feel anything that might mean trouble, check it out.

prompt: In a vehicle with a manual transmission, how do you keep from rolling back when you start?
choices: Rev the engine high and drop the clutch
Release the brake first, then let out the clutch as quickly as possible
Partly engage the clutch before taking your right foot off the brake
Shift into neutral and release the brake
explanation: Partly engage the clutch before taking your right foot off the brake. Use the parking brake when needed to keep from rolling back.

prompt: Your drive wheels begin to spin as you accelerate on a slippery road. What should you do?
choices: Apply the brakes hard
Press harder on the accelerator
Take your foot off the accelerator
Turn the steering wheel sharply
explanation: If the drive wheels spin, take your foot off the accelerator. Speed up very gradually when traction is poor.

prompt: How should you hold the steering wheel?
choices: Firmly, with both hands on opposite sides
With one hand, so the other is free to shift gears
Lightly, with one hand at the top of the wheel
With both hands together at the bottom of the wheel
explanation: Hold the wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides. Hitting a curb or pothole could pull the wheel from a loose grip.

prompt: Why is backing a large vehicle always dangerous?
choices: You cannot see everything behind the vehicle
Reverse gears are weaker than forward gears
Mirrors cannot be used while backing
The brakes work poorly in reverse
explanation: Because you can't see everything behind you, backing is always dangerous. Avoid it when you can and park so you can pull forward when you leave.

prompt: When you must back up, which direction should you back and turn toward whenever possible?
choices: The right (passenger) side
The driver's side
Whichever side has the curb
Away from your helper
explanation: Back toward the driver's side so you can watch the rear by looking out the side window. Backing toward the right is very dangerous because you can't see as well.

prompt: Which hand signal is most important for you and your backing helper to agree on?
choices: Stop
Speed up
Turn left
Straighten out
explanation: Before backing, work out hand signals you both understand, and be sure to agree on a signal for stop.

prompt: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require which shifting technique?
choices: Single clutching at high rpm
Shifting without using the clutch
Pressing the brake while shifting
Double clutching
explanation: Unsynchronized manual transmissions usually require double clutching. Synchronized transmissions do not.

prompt: While double clutching, you stay in neutral too long and can't get into the next gear. What should you do?
choices: Keep pushing the shift lever firmly until it finally slips into the next gear
Coast in neutral until the vehicle has slowed enough to shift
Skip that gear and shift into the next higher gear instead
Return to neutral, release the clutch, match engine to road speed, and retry
explanation: Don't force it. Return to neutral, release the clutch, increase engine speed to match road speed, and try again.

prompt: In which situation does the manual say you should downshift?
choices: Before entering a curve
In the middle of a curve
While braking hard in a curve
Right after leaving a curve
explanation: Slow down and downshift before entering a curve. You can then use some power through the curve to keep the vehicle stable.

prompt: Why should you select a low range on an automatic transmission when going down a grade?
choices: To keep the brakes warm
To get greater engine braking
To let the transmission upshift freely
To save fuel
explanation: A low range gives greater engine braking and keeps the transmission from shifting up past the selected gear.

prompt: When should you turn off your retarder?
choices: When driving on dry highways
When the vehicle is fully loaded with cargo
When the road is wet, icy, or snowy
When starting down a long, steep grade
explanation: On roads with poor traction, a retarder can make the drive wheels skid, so turn it off on wet, icy, or snowy roads.

prompt: What is the main benefit of a retarder?
choices: It keeps the drive wheels from skidding on ice
It adds engine power on hills
It helps slow the vehicle and reduces brake wear
It shortens stopping distance on wet roads
explanation: Retarders help slow the vehicle, reducing the need for the brakes and brake wear. They do not prevent skids and can cause them on slippery roads.

prompt: How far ahead do most good drivers look?
choices: 1 to 2 seconds
20 to 30 seconds
4 to 6 seconds
12 to 15 seconds
explanation: Most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead, while also shifting attention back and forth to things that are closer.

prompt: At highway speed, looking 12 to 15 seconds ahead means looking about how far?
choices: About 100 feet
About one city block
About one full mile
A quarter of a mile
explanation: 12 to 15 seconds is about one block at low speeds and about a quarter of a mile at highway speeds.

prompt: A traffic light ahead has been green for a long time. What should you do?
choices: Change lanes to get around other traffic
Start slowing down and be ready to stop
Speed up to get through before it changes
Keep your speed, since it just stayed green
explanation: A light that has been green a long time will probably change before you get there, so start slowing and be ready to stop.

prompt: When can your mirror adjustment be checked accurately?
choices: At the end of each trip
Only while driving at highway speed
When the vehicle is parked on a slope
When the trailer(s) are straight
explanation: Check mirror adjustment before every trip, and only when the trailer(s) are straight.

prompt: How should each outside mirror be adjusted?
choices: To show only the lane beside you
Pointed as far outward as possible
Tilted up to check overhead clearance
To show some part of your own vehicle
explanation: Each mirror should show some part of the vehicle. This gives you a reference point for judging where other things are.

prompt: When changing lanes, when should you check your mirrors?
choices: Before signaling, and once more when you are halfway across the line
Before, after signaling, after starting, and after finishing the change
Only before you signal, then keep your eyes on the lane ahead
Only once, after the lane change is complete and you are centered
explanation: Check before changing lanes, after signaling, right after you start the change, and after you complete it.

prompt: Compared with a flat mirror, things seen in a convex (curved) mirror appear:
choices: Larger and farther away than they really are
Smaller and farther away than they are
Larger and closer than they really are
The same size, but closer than they really are
explanation: Convex mirrors show a wider area, but everything looks smaller and farther away than it really is. Allow for this.

prompt: What are the three good rules for using turn signals?
choices: Signal only on highways, early, and briefly
Signal briefly, add a hand signal, and cancel early
Signal at the turn, cancel halfway through, and use the horn
Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel after the turn
explanation: Signal well before you turn, keep signaling until the turn is complete, and cancel the signal afterward.

prompt: How should you warn drivers behind you that you'll need to slow down?
choices: Brake suddenly so the drivers behind will notice
Turn on your high beams so they reflect off the car ahead
Tap the brake pedal lightly to flash the brake lights
Wave your arm out the window to signal drivers behind
explanation: A few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, should warn following drivers. Don't stop suddenly.

prompt: A driver behind you wants to pass. Should you signal them when it looks safe?
choices: Yes, if you also flash your headlights
Yes; it is the courteous thing to do
Yes, but only on two-lane roads
No; you could cause a crash and be blamed
explanation: Don't direct traffic. Signaling others to pass could cause a crash, and you could be blamed.

prompt: At dawn, dusk, or in rain or snow, which lights should you use so others can see you?
choices: Identification and clearance lights only
Low-beam headlights
Four-way flashers only
High-beam headlights
explanation: Use your headlights, not just identification or clearance lights, and use low beams. High beams can bother others even in daytime.

prompt: If you must stop on a road or its shoulder, you must put out your emergency warning devices within:
choices: 1 hour
30 minutes
20 minutes
10 minutes
explanation: Warning devices must be put out within ten minutes of stopping on a road or shoulder.

prompt: You stop on a one-way or divided highway. Where should you place your warning devices?
choices: 10 and 100 feet behind, and 100 feet ahead of the vehicle
100, 200, and 500 feet behind the vehicle
10, 100, and 200 feet toward approaching traffic
50, 100, and 150 feet behind the vehicle on the shoulder
explanation: On a one-way or divided highway, place devices 10 feet, 100 feet, and 200 feet toward approaching traffic.

prompt: You stop on a two-lane road with traffic in both directions. Where should your warning devices go?
choices: Within 10 feet of a corner, plus 100 feet behind and 100 feet ahead
One 50 feet ahead of the vehicle and two 50 feet behind it
Two placed 100 feet behind the vehicle and the third one 500 feet behind
At 10, 100, and 200 feet behind the vehicle only, none ahead
explanation: On a two-way or undivided road, place one within 10 feet of the front or rear corner and the others about 100 feet behind and 100 feet ahead.

prompt: You had to stop just past a hill crest that hides your truck from drivers coming up behind. What should you do with the rearmost triangle?
choices: Place it right behind your rear bumper where it's easy for you to watch
Put it on top of the crest only if it is already getting dark outside
Move it back, up to 500 feet, so drivers see it before the hill
Leave it in the cab and rely on your four-way flashers instead
explanation: If a hill, curve, or other obstruction blocks the view, move the rearmost triangle back down the road, up to 500 feet, so drivers get a warning.

prompt: How should you carry warning triangles as you walk out to place them?
choices: Folded flat until you reach each spot
Behind your back so they don't blow away
Between you and the oncoming traffic
Under your arm, facing the road shoulder
explanation: Hold the triangles between yourself and oncoming traffic so other drivers can see you.

prompt: When you pull off the road and stop, what should you turn on?
choices: The interior dome light
Only your taillights
Four-way emergency flashers
High-beam headlights
explanation: Turn on the four-way flashers, especially at night. Don't trust taillights to warn others; drivers have hit parked vehicles thinking they were moving.

prompt: Total stopping distance is made up of which three parts?
choices: Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
Reaction distance, following distance, and braking distance
Signal distance, reaction distance, and coasting distance
Perception distance, following distance, and skid distance
explanation: Perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance = total stopping distance.

prompt: According to the manual, what is the average perception time for an alert driver?
choices: ¼ second
4 seconds
3 seconds
1¾ seconds
explanation: The average perception time for an alert driver is 1¾ seconds, about 142 feet at 55 mph. Reaction time adds another ¾ to 1 second.

prompt: In ideal conditions at 55 mph, what is the minimum total distance a vehicle travels before it stops?
choices: About 216 feet
About 300 feet
About 419 feet
About 142 feet
explanation: At 55 mph: about 142 feet of perception distance, 61 feet of reaction distance, and 216 feet of braking distance, for a total of at least 419 feet.

prompt: At 55 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, about how far does the vehicle travel while braking, not counting perception and reaction?
choices: 419 feet
61 feet
142 feet
216 feet
explanation: Braking distance alone is about 216 feet at 55 mph. Total stopping distance, including perception and reaction, is about 419 feet.

prompt: If you double your speed from 20 mph to 40 mph, your braking distance becomes about:
choices: 2 times longer
3 times longer
8 times longer
4 times longer
explanation: Doubling your speed makes the impact and the braking distance about four times greater, not just twice as great.

prompt: Compared with driving at 20 mph, how much greater are the impact and braking distance at 60 mph?
choices: 4 times greater
3 times greater
9 times greater
6 times greater
explanation: Tripling speed from 20 to 60 mph makes impact and braking distance about 9 times greater. At 80 mph it is 16 times greater.

prompt: Why does an empty truck usually need more distance to stop than a loaded one?
choices: Brakes on empty trucks are designed weaker
Its brakes overheat much faster
It rolls faster on flat roads
An empty vehicle has less traction
explanation: Brakes, tires, springs, and shocks on heavy vehicles work best when fully loaded. An empty truck has less traction, so it needs more distance to stop.

prompt: How much can a wet road increase your stopping distance?
choices: It can double it
About 10 percent
It can triple it
It doesn't change it with good tires
explanation: Wet roads can double stopping distance, so you must drive slower to stop in the same distance as on a dry road.

prompt: On a wet road, how much should you reduce your speed?
choices: By about 5 mph
By about one-third, such as from 55 to about 35 mph
By about 10 percent, such as from 55 to 50 mph
By about one-half, such as from 55 to about 28 mph
explanation: Reduce speed by about one-third on a wet road. On packed snow reduce by half or more, and on ice slow to a crawl.

prompt: On packed snow, you should reduce your speed by:
choices: About one-third
About 10 percent
About 5 mph
Half or more
explanation: On packed snow, reduce speed by a half or more. One-third is the guideline for wet roads.

prompt: When the temperature drops near freezing, which part of the road will freeze first?
choices: Roads in direct sunlight
Roads through towns
Freshly paved roads
Bridges
explanation: Bridges freeze before the road does. Be especially careful when the temperature is close to 32°F.

prompt: What is black ice?
choices: Ice mixed with dirt and road salt that looks dark
Thick ice that forms only at night on shaded roads
Ice hidden under a layer of freshly fallen snow
A thin, clear ice layer that makes the road look wet
explanation: Black ice is clear enough that you can see the road through it, so the road just looks wet. If it's below freezing and the road looks wet, watch for it.

prompt: Which ice is the most slippery?
choices: Ice on a very cold, dry day
Rough, frozen slush in ruts
Ice that has been sanded lightly
Ice that is starting to melt
explanation: Slight melting makes ice wet, and wet ice is much more slippery than ice that is not wet.

prompt: What is an easy way to check whether the road may be starting to ice up?
choices: Tap the brakes hard at highway speed to test traction
Read the outside air temperature on the dashboard
Feel the mirror, mirror support, or antenna for ice
Watch for steam coming out from under the hood
explanation: Open the window and feel the mirror, its support, or the antenna. If there's ice on them, the road is probably starting to ice up.

prompt: Your vehicle starts to hydroplane. How can you regain control?
choices: Accelerate gently to push through the water
Steer sharply toward the shoulder to find grip
Brake firmly and steadily to slow down
Release the accelerator and push in the clutch
explanation: Release the accelerator and push in the clutch so the vehicle slows and the wheels turn freely. Do not use the brakes.

prompt: Hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as:
choices: 30 mph
65 mph
45 mph
55 mph
explanation: If there is a lot of water, hydroplaning can occur at speeds as low as 30 mph.

prompt: A curve is posted at 35 mph and your truck has a high center of gravity. Which statement is true?
choices: Braking mid-curve will keep it stable
The truck could roll over even at 35 mph
35 mph is always safe for trucks
You can safely go 5 mph faster if loaded
explanation: Tests show trucks with a high center of gravity can roll over at the posted speed for a curve. Slow down before the curve as needed.

prompt: When should you slow down for a curve?
choices: Just as you exit it
Before you enter it
In the middle of it
Once you feel the trailer lean
explanation: Slow to a safe speed before entering the curve; braking in a curve can lock the wheels. Be in a gear that lets you accelerate slightly through it.

prompt: What is the number one cause of injury and death in roadway work zones?
choices: Workers stepping into lanes
Speeding traffic
Narrow lanes
Poor lighting
explanation: Speeding traffic is the number one cause of work zone injuries and deaths. Obey the posted limits and don't let your speed creep up.

prompt: You are driving through a work zone and a worker is close to the road. What should you do?
choices: Keep the posted speed and sound your horn
Slow down even more than you already have
Speed up to get past the worker quickly
Move onto the shoulder to give room
explanation: Decrease your speed for bad weather or road conditions, and decrease it even further when a worker is close to the roadway.

prompt: Of all the space around your vehicle, which area is the most important?
choices: The space overhead
The space ahead
The space on the right
The space behind
explanation: The space ahead, the space you're driving into, is the most important.

prompt: According to accident reports, what do trucks and buses most often run into?
choices: A vehicle merging from the right
A vehicle in their blind spot
The vehicle in front of them
A parked vehicle
explanation: Trucks and buses most often hit the vehicle in front of them, and the most frequent cause is following too closely.

prompt: Below 40 mph, how much following distance does the manual recommend?
choices: Two seconds total, no matter how long the vehicle is
At least 1 second for each 10 feet of length
1 second for each 20 feet of vehicle length
1 vehicle length for each 10 mph of speed
explanation: Keep at least one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length below 40 mph, and add 1 second above 40 mph.

prompt: You are driving a 40-foot truck at 55 mph. How many seconds of following distance should you keep?
choices: 6 seconds
5 seconds
4 seconds
3 seconds
explanation: One second per 10 feet gives 4 seconds for 40 feet. Above 40 mph, add 1 second, for a total of 5.

prompt: You are driving a 30-foot vehicle at 55 mph. How much following distance should you allow?
choices: 2 seconds
4 seconds
3 seconds
5 seconds
explanation: A 30-foot vehicle needs 3 seconds; above 40 mph, add 1 second, for 4 seconds.

prompt: How can you measure your following distance?
choices: Divide your speed by ten to get the number of car lengths
Count the seconds until you reach a landmark the vehicle ahead just passed
Count the number of lane stripes between your bumper and the vehicle ahead
Estimate the number of car lengths using your side mirrors
explanation: Wait until the vehicle ahead passes a shadow, marking, or other landmark, then count 'one thousand-and-one...' until you reach the same spot.

prompt: Someone is tailgating you. What should you do?
choices: Turn on your taillights
Increase your following distance
Tap your brakes a few times to warn them
Speed up to get away from them
explanation: Opening up room ahead helps you avoid sudden changes and makes it easier for the tailgater to pass. Don't speed up or use tricks like flashing brake lights.

prompt: A heavy load is slowing you down on an upgrade. What should you do?
choices: Move to the left lane
Pass slower vehicles before the top
Turn on your high beams
Stay in the right lane if you can
explanation: If a heavy load slows you down, stay in the right lane. Going uphill, don't pass another slow vehicle unless you can get around quickly and safely.

prompt: Strong winds make it hard to stay in your lane. Where can this problem be especially bad?
choices: On roads with no shoulder
Coming out of tunnels
In heavy city traffic
On long uphill grades
explanation: Strong winds can be especially bad coming out of tunnels, and the problem is usually worse for lighter vehicles.

prompt: Why shouldn't you trust the heights posted at bridges and overpasses?
choices: Bridges sag several inches in hot weather
Re-paving or packed snow may have reduced the clearance
They are measured at the edge of the road, not the center
They are measured for passenger cars, not trucks
explanation: Re-paving or packed snow may have reduced the clearance since the height was posted. If you aren't sure you can make it, take another route.

prompt: You got under a low bridge while your van trailer was loaded. On the return trip it is empty. What is true?
choices: You will clear it more easily, because the van is lighter
You will clear it, because a van's height doesn't change
You will clear it as long as tire pressure stays the same
You may not clear it, because an empty van rides higher
explanation: An empty van is higher than a loaded one, so getting under a bridge when loaded doesn't mean you can when empty.

prompt: Your truck can't make a right turn without swinging into another lane. How should you turn?
choices: Swing wide to the left first, then turn right from the center
Turn wide as you finish the turn, keeping the rear near the curb
Turn tightly from the curb lane and let the rear wheels ride over the curb
Start the turn from the left lane so you have room to swing
explanation: Turn wide as you complete the turn and keep the rear close to the curb, which stops others from passing on the right.

prompt: During a turn you must cross into the oncoming lane, and a car is approaching. What should you do?
choices: Sound the horn and continue the turn
Give it room to pass or stop, but don't back up
Back up a little to make room for it to pass
Keep turning, because oncoming traffic must yield to you
explanation: Give oncoming vehicles room to go by or to stop. Don't back up for them, because you might hit someone behind you.

prompt: When should you start a left turn?
choices: After you reach the center of the intersection
After your trailer clears the crosswalk
As soon as your front bumper enters the intersection
Before the intersection, to cut the corner
explanation: Reach the center of the intersection before starting a left turn. Turning too soon can make the left side of the vehicle hit something because of off-tracking.

prompt: There are two left-turn lanes. Which one should you use?
choices: Whichever one has less traffic
Either one, as long as you signal
The right-hand (outer) turn lane
The left-hand (inside) turn lane
explanation: Always take the right turn lane. Starting in the inside lane may force you to swing right, and drivers on your left are easier to see.

prompt: In the CDL manual, what is a hazard?
choices: Any road condition or road user that is a possible danger
Only another vehicle that is speeding or weaving
Only an object lying on the road surface
Only a crash or collision that has already happened ahead
explanation: A hazard is any road condition or other road user (driver, bicyclist, pedestrian) that is a possible danger.

prompt: A car ahead brakes hard near an exit as if unsure, then swerves back into your lane in front of you. When did it become an emergency?
choices: When it cut in front of you
When its brake lights first came on
Only if you actually hit it
When it slowed near the exit
explanation: The uncertain car was a hazard. Once it cut in front of you, it became an emergency. Spotting the hazard early gives you time to act.

prompt: Why are off-ramps that go downhill and turn at the same time especially dangerous for trucks?
choices: The downgrade makes slowing hard, and braking while turning is risky
They usually have no lighting, so the curve is hard to see until you're on it
Cars are not allowed to use them, so trucks travel faster
Speed limits are never posted on ramps for large vehicles
explanation: The downgrade makes it hard to slow down, and braking and turning together is dangerous. Posted ramp speeds may be safe for cars but not trucks.

prompt: At a blind alley, you can see the rear end of a vehicle but not its driver. What should you assume?
choices: The driver can't see you either
The driver has seen you in a mirror
The driver will wait for you to pass
The vehicle is parked and empty
explanation: If you can only see part of a vehicle and not the driver, the driver can't see you. Be ready for it to back out or enter your lane.

prompt: What does the 'slow-moving vehicle' symbol look like?
choices: A red triangle with an orange center
A yellow circle with a black X
A red octagon with a white border
An orange diamond with a black border
explanation: The slow-moving vehicle symbol is a red triangle with an orange center. It is used on farm and construction machinery and similar vehicles.

prompt: Which is a clue that a driver may be impaired?
choices: Signaling well before a turn
An open window in cold weather
Driving at a steady speed
Keeping a long following distance
explanation: Clues to impaired drivers include weaving, leaving the road, stopping at the wrong time, an open window in cold weather, and sudden speed changes.

prompt: Which road users' head and body movements give the clearest clues that they are about to turn or change lanes?
choices: Truck drivers
Drivers of tinted-window cars
Motorcyclists and bicyclists
Bus drivers
explanation: Drivers look in the direction they plan to turn, and these clues are most easily seen in motorcyclists and bicyclists.

prompt: Why is an ice cream truck a hazard clue?
choices: Children may be nearby and may not see you
It is likely to back into traffic
It may suddenly speed up
It often has bright lights that cause glare
explanation: Someone selling ice cream is a hazard clue because children may be nearby and may not see you.

prompt: What is a driver distraction?
choices: Anything that takes your attention away from driving
Only using a cell phone
Only events outside the vehicle
Only things that make you take your eyes off the road
explanation: A distraction is anything that takes your attention away from driving, whether inside or outside the vehicle.

prompt: Under the federal rule, which of these is prohibited hand-held phone use while driving a CMV?
choices: Dialing by pressing more than a single button
Using voice-activated dialing
Answering with one touch on a mounted phone
Talking through a hands-free earpiece
explanation: Prohibited use includes holding the phone for a call, dialing by pressing more than a single button, or leaving your belted seated position to reach for the phone.

prompt: Even with a hands-free phone, which action breaks the federal mobile phone rule for CMV drivers?
choices: Talking through an earpiece while keeping both hands on the steering wheel
Using voice-activated dialing to place the call
Using the speakerphone function on a mounted phone
Reaching for the phone so you leave your seated, belted position
explanation: Drivers are not in compliance if they unsafely reach for a phone, even to use its hands-free function. Keep the phone close enough to use while belted.

prompt: When may a CMV driver use a hand-held phone while driving?
choices: For short calls lasting less than one minute
Whenever the phone is set to speaker mode
When stopped briefly in traffic, such as at a red light or stop sign
To contact law enforcement or emergency services when needed
explanation: The only exception is an emergency, when you need to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services.

prompt: A CDL holder gets a second conviction within 3 years for violating a hand-held phone or texting law in a CMV. What is the disqualification?
choices: 60 days
One year
120 days
30 days
explanation: Disqualification is 60 days for a second offense within 3 years and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years.

prompt: Research cited in the manual says texting raises a CMV driver's odds of a safety-critical event by about how much?
choices: 2 times
6 times
23 times
50 times
explanation: Texting raises the odds about 23.2 times. Dialing a phone raises them about 6 times.

prompt: Sending or reading a text takes your eyes off the road for about 4.6 seconds. At 55 mph, how far do you travel?
choices: About 50 feet, roughly a truck length
About one mile
About 371 feet, roughly a football field
About 150 feet, roughly half a block
explanation: At 55 mph, 4.6 seconds without looking means about 371 feet, the length of a football field.

prompt: How do hands-free phones compare with hand-held phones for distraction?
choices: They cause no distraction at all if used with voice commands
They distract you only at night
They are twice as distracting
They are no less likely to distract you
explanation: Hands-free devices are no less likely than hand-held phones to distract you. Attention is taken from driving with either.

prompt: Under the federal rule, what does 'texting' include?
choices: Talking on a hands-free phone
Manually entering or reading text on an electronic device
Only sending text messages from a cell phone, not reading them
Listening to a GPS give spoken directions
explanation: Texting means manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including e-mail, instant messages, and web pages.

prompt: How does road rage differ from aggressive driving?
choices: Aggressive driving always involves a weapon
Road rage involves intent to harm or assault others
Road rage only means changing lanes often and without signaling
There is no difference between the two terms
explanation: Aggressive driving is selfish, pushy driving without regard for others. Road rage is driving with the intent to harm others or assault a driver or vehicle.

prompt: An aggressive driver is tailgating you and gesturing. What should you do first?
choices: Make every attempt to get out of their way
Hold your lane and speed up
Tap your brakes to back them off
Make eye contact so they know you see them
explanation: First, get out of their way. Don't challenge them, avoid eye contact, and ignore gestures.

prompt: An aggressive driver you saw earlier has crashed farther down the road. What should you do?
choices: Park right beside the wreck to help direct traffic around it
Stop a safe distance away, wait for police, and report what you saw
Drive on past without stopping, since the police will handle it
Walk over to the driver and tell them what you thought of their driving
explanation: Stop a safe distance from the crash scene, wait for police, and report the driving behavior you witnessed.

prompt: Your license requires corrective lenses. What does the manual recommend keeping in the vehicle?
choices: A magnifying glass for gauges
Tinted lenses for night driving
An extra set of corrective lenses
A copy of your eye exam
explanation: Keep a spare set of corrective lenses so you can drive safely if your normal pair breaks or is lost.

prompt: With low-beam headlights, about how far ahead can you see?
choices: About 250 feet
About 100 feet
About 1,000 feet
About 500 feet
explanation: Low beams let you see about 250 feet ahead; high beams about 350 to 500 feet. Drive slowly enough to stop within that range.

prompt: With high-beam headlights, about how far ahead can you see?
choices: 350 to 500 feet
150 to 200 feet
About 250 feet
800 to 1,000 feet
explanation: High beams let you see about 350 to 500 feet, compared with about 250 feet for low beams.

prompt: Dirty headlights may give only about how much of the light they should?
choices: Three-quarters
One-tenth
Half
Nine-tenths
explanation: Dirty headlights may give only half the light they should, making it harder for you to see and for others to see you.

prompt: Bright headlights are coming toward you. Where should you look?
choices: Directly at the headlights so you can judge their distance
Slightly to the right, at a lane or edge marking
Down at your instrument panel until they pass
At the center line on your left
explanation: Don't look directly at oncoming lights. Look slightly to the right at a right lane or edge marking, if there is one.

prompt: What is the only safe cure for drowsiness while driving?
choices: Playing loud music
Opening the window
Getting some sleep
Coffee or other caffeine
explanation: If you are drowsy, the only safe cure is to get off the road and get some sleep. Caffeine and fresh air only help briefly.

prompt: According to the manual, how does getting 6 hours of sleep or less affect your crash risk?
choices: It about triples your risk
It has no effect if you drink coffee
It raises it by about 10 percent
It doubles it only at night
explanation: Being sleep-deprived, with 6 hours of sleep or less, triples your risk.

prompt: During long trips, how often does the manual suggest taking breaks?
choices: Only when you need fuel
About every 100 miles or 2 hours
About every 500 miles
About every 300 miles or 6 hours
explanation: Take periodic breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours on long trips.

prompt: You notice signs of fatigue. What does the manual recommend?
choices: Drink extra coffee and keep driving until you feel better
Speed up so you can finish the trip sooner
Open the window and turn up the radio
Sleep for the night, or take a 15–20 minute nap
explanation: Trying to push on is a major cause of fatal accidents. Stop and sleep for the night or take a 15 to 20 minute nap.

prompt: During which hours do many heavy-vehicle crashes occur?
choices: Between midnight and 6 a.m.
Between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m.
Between noon and 3 p.m.
Between 6 a.m. and noon
explanation: Many heavy motor vehicle crashes happen between midnight and 6 a.m., when most people are less alert. Mid-afternoon is another risky time.

prompt: Headlight glare blinds you for 2 seconds while you are going 55 mph. About how far do you travel?
choices: About 20 feet
About a quarter of a mile
More than half the length of a football field
Less than 50 feet, about the length of one tractor-trailer
explanation: Even two seconds of glare blindness is dangerous: at 55 mph you travel more than half a football field.

prompt: What is the best advice for driving in fog?
choices: Don't; wait at a rest area or truck stop until it clears
Follow closely behind the taillights of the vehicle ahead
Drive in the left lane to stay away from parked vehicles
Use your high beams so you can see farther into the fog
explanation: The best advice is not to drive in fog. Pull into a rest area or truck stop until visibility improves.

prompt: If you must drive in fog, which lights should you use?
choices: Clearance lights only
High beams, so you can see farther ahead
Low beams and fog lights, even in daytime
Parking lights only, to reduce glare from the fog
explanation: Use low-beam headlights and fog lights for best visibility, even in daytime.

prompt: According to the manual, why can taillights you see ahead in fog be a poor guide to where the road goes?
choices: Taillights don't have to be lit in fog
Following taillights is illegal in fog
The vehicle may not be on the road at all
Your fog lights hide other vehicles' taillights
explanation: Taillights or headlights ahead may not show where the road is, because the vehicle may be off the road. Use roadside reflectors to judge how the road curves.

prompt: What can happen if the radiator shutters freeze shut or the winterfront is closed too tightly?
choices: The heater will blow too hot
The engine may overheat and stop
The fuel will gel in the lines
The batteries will lose charge
explanation: Remove ice from the radiator shutters and don't close the winterfront too tightly, or the engine may overheat and stop.

prompt: What should you carry and check before driving where tire chains may be needed?
choices: One set of chains for the steering tires only, since they do the steering
Chains sized for the trailer tires only
Any chains, since one size fits all tires
Enough chains and extra cross-links that fit your drive tires
explanation: Carry the right number of chains and extra cross-links, make sure they fit your drive tires, and check for broken hooks and worn links.

prompt: Other vehicles on a wet-looking road are throwing no spray. What does this tell you?
choices: Ice has probably formed on the road
The road was just salted
Traffic is moving too slowly to spray
The road is drying out
explanation: A lack of spray from other vehicles indicates ice has formed. Check your mirrors and wiper blades for ice too.

prompt: You have no choice but to drive through deep standing water. What should you do?
choices: Speed up so you spend as little time as possible in the water
Slow down, use a low gear, and keep light pressure on the brakes
Shift to neutral and coast across
Pump the brakes hard while crossing
explanation: Slow down, shift to a low gear, and gently apply the brakes. Keep light brake pressure and raise engine rpm while crossing so water and mud stay out.

prompt: You have just driven out of deep water. What should you do next?
choices: Keep light brake pressure for a short distance, then do a test stop
Brake hard right away to squeeze the water out of the linings
Pull over and wait about an hour for the brakes to air-dry completely
Drive at highway speed so the wind dries the brakes quickly
explanation: Keep light pressure on the brakes for a short distance to heat and dry them. Then, when safe, check behind you and make a test stop.

prompt: In very hot weather, how often should you inspect your tires?
choices: Every 2 hours or every 100 miles
Every 4 hours or every 200 miles
Only at the start of each day
Every 30 minutes or 25 miles
explanation: Inspect tires every two hours or every 100 miles in very hot weather.

prompt: Your tire pressure has risen during a hot-weather drive. What should you do?
choices: Leave it; letting air out makes it too low when the tire cools
Spray the tire with cold water to cool it
Let air out until the gauge shows the normal cold pressure again
Let out about half of the extra pressure
explanation: Air pressure increases with temperature. Don't let air out, or the pressure will be too low when the tires cool off.

prompt: During a stop in hot weather, a tire is too hot to touch. What should you do?
choices: Spray it with the fire extinguisher
Let some air out and keep going
Drive faster so air cools it
Stay stopped until it cools off
explanation: If a tire is too hot to touch, remain stopped until it cools. Otherwise the tire may blow out or catch fire.

prompt: When is it safe to remove the cap on a pressurized radiator?
choices: Any time the engine is not overheated
Right after you shut off the engine, if you cover the cap with a rag
Only after the system has cooled enough to touch the cap bare-handed
Whenever the temperature gauge reads in the normal range while driving
explanation: Never remove the cap until the system has cooled; steam and boiling water can spray and cause severe burns. If you can touch the cap with a bare hand, it is probably cool enough.

prompt: What is 'bleeding tar'?
choices: Oil leaking from engines and building up on the road surface
Fresh asphalt that the road crew has not yet rolled flat and hardened
Tar that has frozen and cracked open during a cold snap
Tar rising to the surface in hot weather, making the road slippery
explanation: In very hot weather, tar can rise to the surface. Spots where tar bleeds through are very slippery.

prompt: How should you approach every railroad-highway crossing?
choices: Expecting that a train is coming
At the posted speed limit
Relying on the train horn to warn you
Assuming no train is coming unless lights flash
explanation: Railroad crossings are always dangerous. Approach every one expecting a train.

prompt: What does the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign for a railroad crossing tell you?
choices: You must stop at the sign every time, even if no train is near
The crossing ahead is protected by gates
Slow down, look and listen, and be ready to stop for a train
A train is approaching the crossing right now
explanation: The advance warning sign tells you to slow down, look and listen for a train, and be prepared to stop at the tracks.

prompt: If there is no white stop line, how far from the nearest rail must a vehicle that is required to stop at a crossing stop?
choices: No closer than 5 feet and no farther than 25 feet
No closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet
No closer than 50 feet and no farther than 100 feet
No closer than 25 feet and no farther than 75 feet
explanation: Vehicles required to stop must stop no closer than 15 feet and no more than 50 feet from the nearest rail.

prompt: At a crossing with gates, when may you go across after a train passes?
choices: When the bell stops ringing
When the gates start to rise
As soon as the last car of the train passes the crossing
After the gates go up and the lights stop flashing
explanation: Remain stopped until the gates go up and the lights stop flashing. Then proceed when it is safe.

prompt: A train has just passed a double-track crossing. What should you do before starting across?
choices: Sound your horn and then cross
Go right away while the gates are still up and the lights are off
Make sure no other train is coming on the other track
Wait exactly 30 seconds, then cross
explanation: A train on one track may hide a train on the other. After one train clears, be sure no other trains are near before crossing.

prompt: About how long does it take a typical tractor-trailer to clear a single track?
choices: About 8 seconds
About 5 seconds
About 30 seconds
At least 14 seconds
explanation: A typical tractor-trailer needs at least 14 seconds to clear a single track and more than 15 seconds for a double track.

prompt: What should you NOT do while driving across railroad tracks?
choices: Shift gears
Look both ways
Keep a steady speed
Check your mirrors
explanation: Do not shift gears while crossing tracks. Make sure you can get all the way across before you start.

prompt: Which vehicle is most likely to get stuck on a raised railroad crossing?
choices: A dump truck with high clearance
A lowboy or car carrier
A straight box truck
A tractor with no trailer
explanation: Low-slung units such as lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, and possum-belly livestock trailers can hang up on raised crossings.

prompt: Your truck gets stuck on the tracks. What should you do?
choices: Stay in the cab, turn on the flashers, and sound the horn
Stay in the cab and keep trying to back up or drive off the tracks until free
Walk down the tracks toward the train to wave it down
Get out and away from the tracks, then call the posted number or 911
explanation: Get out of the vehicle and away from the tracks. Check the signpost or signal housing for emergency information, call, and give the location, including the DOT number if posted.

prompt: What does a cross-buck sign at a railroad crossing require you to do?
choices: Watch for a flagger
Yield the right-of-way to trains
Speed up to clear the tracks quickly
Stop every time
explanation: The cross-buck marks the crossing and requires you to yield the right-of-way to the train. A sign below it shows the number of tracks.

prompt: What is brake fade?
choices: Brakes that were adjusted too tightly at the last service
Brake linings wearing out slowly from age and normal use
Hot brakes needing more and more pressure to slow the vehicle
Brake lights getting dim, so drivers behind you can't see them well
explanation: When brakes get too hot, you must apply them harder and harder to get the same stopping power. They can fade until you cannot stop at all.

prompt: When should you shift into a low gear for a long downgrade?
choices: Once your speed starts to build
Halfway down the grade
When the brakes begin to fade
Before you start down the grade
explanation: Shift to a low gear before starting down. After speed builds you may not be able to downshift, and you could lose all engine braking.

prompt: Why might a modern truck need a lower gear going down a hill than it used to climb it?
choices: Low-friction parts and streamlined shapes leave less drag to slow it
Modern brakes are designed to be used less
Modern engines have much less braking power than the engines in older trucks
The law requires a lower gear on all downgrades
explanation: Modern trucks can climb in higher gears and have less friction and air drag holding them back downhill, so they may need lower gears going down.

prompt: Your 'safe' speed on a downgrade is 40 mph. What is the proper braking technique?
choices: Pump the brakes rapidly every few seconds all the way down
Let speed build to 50 mph, then brake back down to 40 mph
At 40 mph, brake to about 35 mph, release, and repeat as needed
Hold light, steady pressure on the brake pedal the whole way down the grade
explanation: Once in the proper low gear, apply the brakes for a definite slowdown to about 5 mph below your safe speed, then release. Repeat each time you reach the safe speed.

prompt: Using the proper downgrade braking technique, about how long should each brake application last?
choices: About 10 seconds
About 30 seconds
About 1 minute
About 3 seconds
explanation: Each application, bringing speed down about 5 mph below the safe speed, should last about three seconds.

prompt: How can brakes that are out of adjustment lead to brake fade?
choices: They grab hard and lock the wheels every time you use them on a grade
They make the ABS switch off
They cause the engine to lose power
They stop doing their share, so the other brakes overheat
explanation: Every brake must do its share. Out-of-adjustment brakes quit working before the others, which then overheat and fade.

prompt: What are truck escape ramps designed to do?
choices: Give truck drivers a safe place to pull off and test their brakes
Stop runaway vehicles safely with soft, loose material
Provide parking for drivers who need to rest
Let slow trucks get out of the way of faster traffic
explanation: Escape ramps use a long bed of loose, soft material, sometimes with an upgrade, to stop runaway vehicles without injuring the occupants.

prompt: When making a quick turn to avoid a crash, what should you do?
choices: Brake hard while you turn
Turn as sharply as you can
Avoid braking while you turn
Take one hand off the wheel to signal
explanation: Don't brake while turning, since it's easy to lock the wheels and skid. Turn only as much as needed to clear the obstacle.

prompt: What is counter-steering?
choices: Turning back the other way once you have passed the obstacle
Steering opposite to the way you actually want to go
Steering toward the direction of the skid
Turning the wheel quickly back and forth to keep the tires gripping
explanation: Counter-steering is turning back the other way after passing what was in your path. Think of the emergency steer and counter-steer as one action.

prompt: An oncoming driver has drifted into your lane. Which way should you steer?
choices: Into the oncoming lane
Straight ahead while braking hard
To your left
To your right
explanation: Move to your right. If the other driver realizes the mistake, the natural response is to return to their own lane.

prompt: Something blocks your path and both sides are also blocked. Which way may be best to steer?
choices: To the right
To the left
Whichever side has more traffic
Straight into the obstacle
explanation: If blocked on both sides, a move to the right may be best. At least you won't force anyone into opposing traffic and a possible head-on crash.

prompt: You must leave the road in an emergency. When should you start braking?
choices: Not until the vehicle is back on the road
Only after all of the wheels are off the pavement
Not until speed drops to about 20 mph, then brake gently
Immediately, and as hard as possible, so you stop before anything
explanation: Avoid braking until speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake very gently to avoid skidding on the loose surface.

prompt: You must return to the road from the shoulder before you can stop. How should you do it?
choices: Turn sharply back on, then counter-steer when both front tires are on
Brake hard on the shoulder first, then steer back on
Return with only the rear wheels on the pavement
Ease back onto the pavement gradually, a little at a time, over a long distance
explanation: Don't edge back gradually; the tires might grab and you could lose control. Turn sharply, then counter-steer immediately as one steer-counter-steer move.

prompt: What is controlled braking?
choices: Using only the parking brake
Pumping the brakes slowly and gently
Braking fully, releasing when the wheels lock, and repeating
Braking as hard as you can without locking the wheels
explanation: In controlled braking you brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels and keep steering movements very small.

prompt: When using stab braking, when should you re-apply the brakes fully?
choices: Right after releasing, before the wheels roll
Only after the vehicle has stopped skidding sideways
After waiting five seconds
As soon as the wheels start rolling again
explanation: Apply fully, release when the wheels lock, and re-apply as soon as they start rolling. It can take up to a second; re-applying too soon keeps the vehicle from straightening.

prompt: Your hydraulic brake pedal goes to the floor. Which actions can help?
choices: Downshift, pump the brakes, and use the parking brake
Shut off the engine and coast to a stop
Shift into neutral and steer onto the shoulder to coast
Hold the pedal down hard and wait for it to catch
explanation: With loss of hydraulic pressure, downshift, pump the brake pedal to build pressure, and use the parking brake, which is a separate system.

prompt: When using the parking brake to slow down after hydraulic brake failure, what should you do?
choices: Apply it in short, sharp jerks
Hold the release button or lever so you can control the pressure
Apply it only after you have shifted into neutral
Pull it on as hard as you can, all at once, and keep it there until you stop
explanation: Press the release button or pull the release lever while applying the emergency brake so you can adjust pressure and keep the wheels from locking.

prompt: Your brakes fail on a long downgrade and there is an escape ramp ahead. What should you do?
choices: Pump the brakes and try to stop on the shoulder
Pass it and try to stop at the bottom
Use the escape ramp to stop the truck
Use it only if there is no traffic
explanation: Any driver who loses brakes going downhill should use an escape ramp if available. Not using it may make a serious crash much more likely.

prompt: The steering suddenly feels heavy. What is this probably a sign of?
choices: The trailer is overloaded
A rear tire has failed
A front tire has failed
The power steering fluid is too full
explanation: Heavy steering is probably a sign that a front tire has failed. Heavy vibration or thumping may be the only sign of a rear tire failure.

prompt: A tire blows out. Unless you are about to hit something, how should you use the brakes?
choices: Pump the brakes rapidly to keep the wheels from locking
Use only the parking brake
Stay off them until the vehicle slows, then brake gently
Brake hard right away to stop as quickly as possible
explanation: Braking when a tire has failed could cause loss of control. Hold the wheel firmly, stay off the brake until the vehicle slows, then brake gently and pull off.

prompt: After a tire failure, you come to a stop and the vehicle seems to handle fine. What should you do?
choices: Keep driving, since it seems fine
Get out and check all the tires
Wait until the next inspection
Check only the steering tires
explanation: Check all the tires even if the vehicle seems fine. If one of your dual tires has failed, looking may be the only way to know.

prompt: Does ABS shorten your stopping distance?
choices: No, it always makes stopping distance longer
Not necessarily, but it helps you keep control
Yes, it always cuts stopping distance about in half
Yes, but only on dry pavement
explanation: ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control and steer while braking hard.

prompt: Truck tractors with air brakes are required to have ABS if they were built on or after:
choices: March 1, 1999
January 1, 1995
March 1, 1997
March 1, 1998
explanation: ABS is required on air-braked truck tractors built on or after March 1, 1997, and on other air-braked vehicles built on or after March 1, 1998.

prompt: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 lbs or more are required to have ABS if built on or after:
choices: January 1, 2001
March 1, 1998
March 1, 1997
March 1, 1999
explanation: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses of 10,000 lbs GVWR or more built on or after March 1, 1999 must have ABS.

prompt: Where is the ABS malfunction lamp on a trailer?
choices: On the rear doors, near the license plate
On the right side, near the landing gear
On the left side, at the front or rear corner
On the tractor's dashboard only, not the trailer
explanation: Trailers have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner. Tractors, trucks, and buses have them on the instrument panel.

prompt: On some older ABS systems, how long may the malfunction lamp stay on after start-up?
choices: Until the engine reaches operating temperature
For the first 10 minutes of driving
Until the air pressure reaches 60 psi
Until you are driving over 5 mph
explanation: On newer vehicles the lamp comes on briefly for a bulb check. On older systems it could stay on until you are driving over five mph.

prompt: In an emergency stop, when may you fully apply the brakes?
choices: Whenever the tractor has ABS, even if the trailer does not
Never; a vehicle with ABS must always be braked lightly, even in emergencies
Whenever only the trailer has working ABS
In a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles
explanation: Normally brake as you always have. The one exception: with working ABS on all axles of a straight truck or combination, you can fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.

prompt: Your ABS malfunction lamp comes on while you are driving. What should you do?
choices: Brake normally and have the system serviced soon
Brake only with the parking brake
Brake much harder than usual for the rest of the trip
Stop at once and wait for a tow truck
explanation: If ABS fails, you still have normal brakes. Drive and brake normally, but get the system serviced soon.

prompt: Which type of skid will ABS NOT prevent?
choices: Wheel lockup during a hard emergency stop
A jackknife caused by over-braking the tractor
One caused by braking too hard and locking up the wheels on ice
One caused by spinning the drive wheels or turning too fast
explanation: ABS should prevent brake-induced skids and jackknifes, but not skids caused by spinning the drive wheels or going too fast in a turn.

prompt: Only your tractor has ABS. What should you watch for while braking?
choices: The trailer wheels locking only at low speed
The trailer swinging out; ease off the brakes if safe
The tractor ABS lamp turning green
The steering wheel locking up in your hands during the stop
explanation: With tractor-only ABS you should keep steering control and have less chance of jackknifing, but watch the trailer and ease off the brakes if it starts to swing out.

prompt: According to the manual, most serious skids result from:
choices: Worn brake linings on the drive axle
Heavy crosswinds
Driving too fast for road conditions
Low tire pressure on the trailer
explanation: Skids come from over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, or driving too fast. Most serious skids result from driving too fast for conditions.

prompt: What is by far the most common type of skid?
choices: A skid caused by a tire blowout
A skid where the drive wheels lose traction
A front-wheel skid caused by worn steering tires
A trailer skid caused by strong side winds
explanation: The most common skid is a drive-wheel skid, where the rear wheels lose traction through too much braking or acceleration.

prompt: How can you stop a skid caused by too much acceleration on ice?
choices: Accelerate a bit harder so the drive tires can dig in and regain traction
Take your foot off the gas, and push in the clutch if very slippery
Turn the wheel sharply in either direction
Brake firmly and steadily until the skid stops
explanation: Taking your foot off the accelerator can easily stop it. On a very slippery road, push in the clutch so the wheels can roll freely.

prompt: How do you correct a drive-wheel braking skid?
choices: Stop braking, then counter-steer as it comes back on course
Brake harder until the vehicle comes to a full stop
Accelerate and steer away from the direction of the skid
Apply the parking brake and hold the steering wheel straight
explanation: Stop braking so the rear wheels roll again, and be ready to counter-steer quickly so you don't skid the other way.

prompt: In a front-wheel skid, what does the front of the vehicle tend to do?
choices: Bounce up and down
Go straight no matter how you steer
Pull sharply to the right side of the road
Spin around toward the rear
explanation: In a front-wheel skid, the front end tends to go straight regardless of steering, so you may not be able to steer around a curve.

prompt: What is the only way to stop a front-wheel skid?
choices: Speed up to shift weight onto the front
Turn the wheel harder in the direction you want the vehicle to go
Brake as hard as you can
Let the vehicle slow down; ease off turning and/or hard braking
explanation: The only way to stop a front-wheel skid is to let the vehicle slow down. Stop turning and/or braking so hard, and slow as quickly as possible without skidding.

prompt: What are the three basic steps to take at any accident scene?
choices: Care for the injured, move them away, and call your company
Call your dispatcher, wait for the tow truck, and clean up the debris
Protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured
Move all vehicles off the road, take photos, and then leave
explanation: At any accident, protect the area, notify authorities, and care for the injured.

prompt: You stop to help at an accident you were not involved in. Where should you park?
choices: In the lane behind the wreck
In front of the wreck to block traffic
Right next to the damaged vehicles
Away from the accident
explanation: Park away from the accident, because the area around it will be needed for emergency vehicles. Turn on flashers and set out triangles.

prompt: If you have a phone or CB radio at an accident, when should you call for help?
choices: After you set out the triangles
Before you get out of your vehicle
Only after you have helped the injured
After the police arrive
explanation: If you have a phone or CB, call for help before getting out. If not, protect the scene first, then call or send someone.

prompt: When should you move a severely injured person at an accident scene?
choices: Only after giving them something to drink
Whenever they ask you to help them move
Only if fire or passing traffic makes it necessary
Always, right away, so that they are off the road and out of traffic
explanation: Don't move a severely injured person unless the danger of fire or passing traffic makes it necessary.

prompt: How should you stop heavy bleeding from a wound?
choices: Pour water over the wound
Apply direct pressure to the wound
Wait for the bleeding to stop on its own
Raise the person's feet only
explanation: Stop heavy bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound, and keep the injured person warm.

prompt: Which is a common cause of tire fires?
choices: Tires that were recently replaced or rotated
Under-inflated tires and duals that touch
Driving on wet roads for a long time
Tires with too much tread for the season
explanation: Under-inflated tires and duals that touch can cause tire fires. Check tires, wheels, and the body for signs of heat at every stop.

prompt: Your truck catches fire. Where should you stop?
choices: In an open area away from buildings, trees, and brush
Next to a building that has a water supply
At the nearest service station, where help is available
Under an overpass to shelter the vehicle from wind
explanation: Pull off in an open area away from anything that might catch fire. Don't pull into a service station, and notify emergency services.

prompt: How should you handle an engine fire?
choices: Pour water into the air intake
Keep the engine running so the fan can cool it
Open the hood all the way so you can reach the flames directly
Turn off the engine and avoid opening the hood if you can
explanation: Turn off the engine as soon as you can and don't open the hood if you can avoid it. Shoot extinguishing agent through louvers, the radiator, or from underneath.

prompt: There is a fire in the cargo of your box trailer. What should you do with the doors?
choices: Open them to reach the fire
Open them to let smoke out
Open them only if the cargo is hazardous
Keep them shut to limit oxygen
explanation: Keep the doors shut, especially with hazardous materials. Opening them supplies oxygen and can make the fire burn very fast.

prompt: When using a fire extinguisher, where should you aim?
choices: Around the outer edges of the fire
Up into the tallest flames
At the thickest smoke
At the base of the fire
explanation: Aim at the source or base of the fire, not up in the flames, and stay as far away as possible.

prompt: What types of fire is a B:C extinguisher designed for?
choices: Electrical fires and burning liquids
Tire fires only
Burning metals
Only wood, paper, and cloth fires (ordinary combustibles)
explanation: A B:C extinguisher works on electrical fires and burning liquids. An A:B:C type also works on wood, paper, and cloth.

prompt: Why shouldn't you use water on a gasoline fire?
choices: It will make the fuel explode
It will spread the flames
It reacts with gasoline to make poison gas
It can cause an electric shock
explanation: Water spreads the flames of a gasoline fire, and on an electrical fire it can cause shock. Water is fine for wood, paper, or cloth.

prompt: How do you put out a burning tire?
choices: Let air out of the tire
Cover it with a tarp
Drive on so the wind blows it out
Cool it; lots of water may be needed
explanation: A burning tire must be cooled, and lots of water may be required.

prompt: The smoke and flames are gone after you use your extinguisher. What should you do?
choices: Open the doors or hood so the area can air out and cool down
Drive on to the next town and report it to the fire department
Stop, since no smoke or flame means the fire is out
Keep going until it has cooled, since it can restart
explanation: Continue until the burning material has cooled. No smoke or flame doesn't mean the fire can't restart.

prompt: Which kind of fire is a Class D fire?
choices: Gasoline and grease
Burning metals
Wood and paper
Electrical equipment
explanation: Class D fires involve combustible metals and need special extinguishing powders. Class A is ordinary combustibles, B is flammable liquids, and C is electrical.
