prompt: What will sober up a person who has been drinking?
choices: Black coffee
Only time
Fresh air and exercise
A cold shower
explanation: The liver processes alcohol at a fixed rate, so only time will sober you up, not coffee or a cold shower.

prompt: Which drinks contain about the same amount of alcohol?
choices: 12 oz of 5% beer, 12 oz of 12% wine, and 12 oz of 80-proof liquor
6 oz of beer, 10 oz of wine, and 3 oz of 80-proof liquor
24 oz of beer, 5 oz of wine, and 1 oz of 80-proof liquor
12 oz of 5% beer, 5 oz of 12% wine, 1½ oz of 80-proof liquor
explanation: A 12-ounce 5% beer, a 5-ounce 12% wine, and a 1½-ounce shot of 80-proof liquor all have the same amount of alcohol.

prompt: When may a CMV driver use a prescription drug while on duty?
choices: Any time it was prescribed by a licensed doctor
Never; all drugs are banned while on duty
When a doctor says it won't affect safe driving
Only on trips shorter than 100 miles
explanation: Possession and use of a doctor-prescribed drug is allowed if the doctor informs the driver it will not affect safe driving ability.

prompt: You become ill while on the road. What does the manual say?
choices: Take extra medicine and continue
Keep driving if your load is due, but take more frequent breaks
Don't drive, except to the nearest safe place in an emergency
Drive slower than normal to finish the trip
explanation: If you're too ill to drive safely, you must not drive. In an emergency, you may drive to the nearest place where you can safely stop.

prompt: According to the manual, about how much alcohol can the liver process per hour?
choices: About one full ounce
About two standard drinks
About one-third of an ounce
About 3 ounces
explanation: The liver can process only about one-third of an ounce of alcohol per hour, less than the alcohol in a standard drink.

prompt: What are hazardous materials?
choices: Any liquid carried in a tank
Any cargo weighing more than 10,000 pounds, no matter what it is
Products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property
Only explosives, poisons, and radioactive materials shipped in bulk
explanation: Hazardous materials are products that pose a risk to health, safety, and property during transportation.

prompt: Where must hazardous materials shipping papers be kept while you are driving?
choices: In the sleeper berth, where they stay clean and dry
With the cargo inside the trailer so they stay with the load
In a pouch on the driver's door or in clear view within reach
Locked in the glove box
explanation: Keep hazmat shipping papers in a pouch on the driver's door or in clear view within reach while driving.

prompt: When you leave the vehicle, where should hazardous materials shipping papers be?
choices: In your pocket
On the driver's seat
Locked in the trailer
In the sleeper berth
explanation: When you are out of the vehicle, the shipping papers should be on the driver's seat so emergency responders can find them.

prompt: How many placards must a placarded vehicle display, and where?
choices: At least four identical placards: front, rear, and both sides
Two placards, one on each side of the trailer
Two placards, one on the front bumper and one on the rear doors
One placard, on the driver's door
explanation: A placarded vehicle must have at least four identical placards, on the front, rear, and both sides, readable from all four directions.

prompt: How are hazardous materials identification numbers written?
choices: Four-digit codes preceded by 'UN' or 'NA'
The hazard class number alone
Two-letter state codes
Six-digit codes preceded by 'DOT' and the class
explanation: Identification numbers are four-digit codes used by first responders, preceded by the letters UN or NA.

prompt: Your truck carries a small amount of hazardous material that does not require placards. Do you need a hazardous materials endorsement?
choices: Yes; any amount of hazardous material requires it
Yes, unless the trip is under 50 miles
No; it is needed only when placards are required
No, as long as your employer gives permission
explanation: You can drive a vehicle carrying hazardous materials if it doesn't require placards. If it requires placards, you need the hazardous materials endorsement.

prompt: When is a tank endorsement required for a tank designed to carry liquid or gas?
choices: Only tanks totaling 10,000 gallons or more
Only tanks that are carrying hazardous materials
Individual tanks over 119 gallons, totaling 1,000 gallons or more
Any single tank holding more than 50 gallons, no matter the total capacity
explanation: A tank endorsement is needed for tanks with an individual rated capacity over 119 gallons and an aggregate of 1,000 gallons or more. The contents don't have to be hazardous.

prompt: Which book lists hazardous chemicals and the identification numbers assigned to them?
choices: The state driver handbook
The Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards
The truck's owner's manual
The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
explanation: The US DOT Emergency Response Guidebook lists chemicals and their identification numbers.

prompt: Gasoline and acetone belong to which hazard class?
choices: Class 3, Flammable liquids
Class 2, Gases
Class 8, Corrosives
Class 4, Flammable solids
explanation: Class 3 is flammable liquids, such as gasoline and acetone. Class 2 is gases, like propane.

prompt: If someone else loads and secures your cargo, who is responsible for inspecting it?
choices: Only the person who loaded it
Only the shipper
You, the driver
Only the receiver
explanation: Whether or not you load and secure the cargo yourself, you are responsible for inspecting it, recognizing overloads and poor balance, and knowing it is secured.

prompt: Besides checking cargo every 3 hours or 150 miles, when else should you re-check it?
choices: After every break you take during driving
Only at the end of the trip
Only when you cross a state line or enter a weigh station
Only after driving on rough roads
explanation: Re-check cargo and securing devices after every break you take during driving, as well as after 3 hours or 150 miles.

prompt: What is the Gross Vehicle Weight Rating (GVWR)?
choices: The weight of the vehicle when it is empty, without fuel or cargo
The most weight a tire can carry
The weight carried by one axle
The manufacturer's specified loaded weight of a single vehicle
explanation: GVWR is the value specified by the manufacturer as the loaded weight of a single vehicle.

prompt: Where can you find a tire's maximum safe load rating?
choices: On the vehicle registration
On the side of the tire
On the bill of lading
On the dashboard label
explanation: Tire load is the maximum safe weight a tire can carry at a specified pressure, and it is stated on the side of each tire.

prompt: What does a bridge formula do?
choices: It allows less weight on axles that are closer together
It sets the height clearance posted at overpasses
It sets lower speed limits for trucks crossing bridges
It allows more weight on axles that are closer together
explanation: A bridge formula permits less maximum axle weight for axles that are closer together, to prevent overloading bridges and roads.

prompt: How can overloading affect your vehicle?
choices: It improves traction and shortens stopping distance
It only matters when crossing bridges
It hurts steering, braking, and speed control
It only affects your fuel mileage
explanation: Overloading has bad effects on steering, braking, and speed control. Stopping distance increases and brakes can fail when forced to work too hard.

prompt: How should you load cargo to reduce the chance of tipping over?
choices: Stack it as high as possible to save floor space
Put the heaviest parts on top to hold the rest down
Keep it low, with the heaviest parts under the lightest
Put most of the weight on one side
explanation: A high center of gravity makes rollover more likely. Distribute cargo as low as possible with the heaviest parts under the lightest.

prompt: What can happen if there is too much weight on the steering axle?
choices: Poor traction at the drive wheels on wet roads
The trailer swinging out on curves
Steering that becomes much too light to control the vehicle safely
Hard steering and damage to the steering axle and tires
explanation: Too much weight on the steering axle can cause hard steering and damage the steering axle and tires.

prompt: What can happen if there is too little weight on the drive axles?
choices: A higher center of gravity and rollover
Overheated brakes on the steering axle when stopping
Poor traction, so the drive wheels may spin
Hard steering at low speeds
explanation: Too little weight on the driving axles can cause poor traction, and in bad weather the truck may not be able to keep going.

prompt: In cargo securement, what is bracing?
choices: Supports running from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls
A tarp tied tightly over the top of the load
Chains that run over the top of the cargo to the side rails
Wooden pieces fitted snugly against the bottom of the cargo on the deck
explanation: Bracing goes from the upper part of the cargo to the floor and/or walls of the cargo compartment. Blocking, by contrast, is fitted snugly against the front, back, or sides of the cargo and secured to the deck.

prompt: Under federal rules, the total working load limit of the tie-downs securing an article must be at least:
choices: One-tenth the weight of the article
One-half the weight of the article
Equal to twice the weight of the article
One-quarter the weight of the article
explanation: The aggregate working load limit of the securement system must be at least one-half the weight of the article or group of articles.

prompt: Using the manual's rule of thumb, how many tie-downs should a 30-foot load have at minimum?
explanation: The manual's rule of thumb is at least one tie-down for each 10 feet of cargo, so a 30-foot load needs at least three. (Federal rules in 49 CFR 393.110 can require more for long articles.)

prompt: According to the CDL manual, what is the minimum number of tie-downs any cargo should have, no matter how small it is?
explanation: The manual says that no matter how small the cargo, it should have at least two tie-downs, plus at least one for each 10 feet of cargo.

prompt: What does a front-end header board (headache rack) do?
choices: Keeps the tarp from flapping in the wind
Protects you from cargo moving forward in a crash
Improves the truck's aerodynamics and cuts fuel use at highway speed
Holds the spare tire and tire chains
explanation: Header boards protect you from your cargo in a crash or emergency stop, so the front-end structure should block forward movement of the cargo.

prompt: What are the two basic reasons for covering cargo?
choices: To hide the cargo from thieves and to reduce wind drag
To protect people from spills and the cargo from weather
To make the load look neat and to keep birds off it
To keep the cargo clean and to meet state weight limits
explanation: Cover cargo to protect people from spills and to protect the cargo from weather. Check covers in your mirrors while driving.

prompt: You can't inspect a sealed load. What should you still check?
choices: That the total load weighs less than 10,000 pounds, including pallets
That the cargo inside is covered with a tarp
That the seal has the shipper's logo and today's date
That you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits
explanation: You cannot inspect sealed loads, but you should check that you don't exceed gross weight and axle weight limits.

prompt: Why does hanging meat in a refrigerated trailer need special caution?
choices: It is much heavier than other refrigerated loads, so it overloads the axles
It has a high center of gravity and is very unstable on sharp curves
It shifts only when you accelerate hard
It can spoil if you drive too slowly
explanation: Hanging meat can be a very unstable load with a high center of gravity. Go slowly, especially on sharp curves such as on and off ramps.

prompt: When hauling less than a full load of livestock, what should you use?
choices: A tarp over the top of the trailer
False bulkheads to keep the animals bunched together
A higher gear to keep your speed up on curves
Extra tie-down straps fastened around each of the animals
explanation: Use false bulkheads to keep livestock bunched. Even then, animals can lean on curves, shifting the center of gravity and making rollover more likely.

prompt: What do over-length, over-width, or overweight loads require?
choices: Special transit permits
A second driver at all times
Nothing beyond a normal CDL
A hazardous materials endorsement
explanation: Oversized loads require special transit permits and may need signs, lights, flags, escorts, or pilot vehicles. Driving times are usually limited.

prompt: Some drivers use low-beam headlights all the time at night. What does the manual say about this?
choices: It is the safest habit for truck drivers
It is required by federal law for CMVs
It is a mistake; use high beams when safe and legal
It only matters when driving in fog
explanation: Always using low beams seriously cuts down how far you can see. Use high beams when it is safe and legal, and dim them before they cause glare for other drivers.

prompt: When you are driving in heavy traffic, what is usually the safest speed?
choices: About 10 mph slower than everyone else
The speed of other traffic, if legal and safe
Fast enough to keep passing slower vehicles
The minimum speed posted for the road
explanation: In heavy traffic the safest speed is the speed of other vehicles, without going at an illegal or unsafe speed. Driving faster means constant passing, which raises crash risk and fatigue.

prompt: The road makes your truck tilt so its top could hit signs or tree limbs at the edge. What should you do?
choices: Drive a little closer to the center of the road
Move closer to the right edge so you are out of traffic
Speed up so the vehicle levels out
Let some air out of the tires on the high side
explanation: Some roads make a vehicle tilt, which can make it hard to clear signs, trees, or bridge supports along the edge. Where this is a problem, drive a little closer to the center of the road.

prompt: Your truck is heavily loaded and you need to cross or enter traffic. What gap do you need?
choices: The same gap you would use in a car
A smaller gap, since other drivers will slow for a truck
A much larger gap than in a car, and more when loaded
Any gap, because merging trucks have the right-of-way
explanation: Large vehicles accelerate slowly and need more space, so you may need a much larger gap than in a car. Acceleration varies with the load, so allow more room when heavily loaded.

prompt: Why is steering away sometimes better than stopping in an emergency?
choices: You can almost always turn to miss something faster than you can stop
Braking is not allowed once a crash is likely
Swerving never causes a rollover, even in a top-heavy truck
Steering keeps the wheels from locking even while braking hard
explanation: When there isn't room to stop, you can almost always turn to miss an obstacle more quickly than you can stop. Top-heavy vehicles and tractors with multiple trailers may still flip over.

prompt: When does an antilock braking system (ABS) come into action?
choices: Every time you press the brake pedal
Only when the wheels are about to lock up
Only when the parking brake is set
Whenever the vehicle is over 55 mph
explanation: ABS is an addition to your normal brakes and only activates when wheels are about to lock up. At all other times the brakes work normally.

prompt: Why are exhaust system leaks especially dangerous in winter?
choices: Cold air makes leaking pipes catch fire
Leaking exhaust melts snow onto the brakes
With windows closed, carbon monoxide can build up in the cab
Exhaust leaks make the heater stop working
explanation: Exhaust leaks are especially dangerous when cab ventilation is poor, such as with windows rolled up. Carbon monoxide makes you sleepy and in large enough amounts can kill you.
